name: BAG SEAL, GUSSET OR PATCH FAILURE

spot.v: Mould starting at a break in the bottom gusset or at the top seal while the rest of the bag is well colonized. Sporadic across a batch, always at the same spots.

look.v: Many colours across the lot is air, not bags. All blocks from one spawn bag is spawn.

cause.v: Uneven or weak seals, seals too hot (micro-perforations, mainly the top seal after inoculation), filter patches with defects. Bag makers change plastic often. Problems can hide in a very clean facility.

treat.v: Seal test: the film must tear before the seal does. Squeeze test: a sealed A-patch bag should let little air out. Change bag lot or supplier.

prevent.v: Test every new bag lot (seal, squeeze, gussets, patches). B patches pass air quickly, which alone does not mean more Neurospora risk.

risk.v: Not species-specific. Mostly Neurospora or other moulds follow.

spot.v: Patchy contamination across the batch with many types and uneven colonization and yield. Sporadic chunky spots over about 2 weeks in some bags. Strong top and weak or airless bottom on big blocks.

look.v: Outer blocks in an over-packed barrel dried and poor, inner ones fine, is overcooking, not contamination.

cause.v: Core of the hardest-to-heat block not held above 93 °C (200 °F) long enough, or an over-packed barrel whose inner blocks stay cold. Textbook: at least 2-3 h, at most 4-6 h, measured. The farm plan holds 4 h (Joseph, 5 Nov 2026).

treat.v: Raise the temperature or extend the hold, log the core with a thermocouple, and discard the affected blocks.

prevent.v: Start with the cook logger record before changing anything else. Moulds die by about 66 °C (150 °F); endospores need pressure.

risk.v: Shiitake can look fine all the way and fail late from an undercook.

spot.v: Rainbow moulds or Neurospora a few days after knocking, racks nearest a door or window worst. Hot blocks left waiting 1-3 days give weak, greasy growth.

look.v: A cook failure shows as patchy, many types, uneven yield; a dirty cool-down shows many colours with otherwise good colonization.

cause.v: Most widespread contamination comes from improper cool-down. Bags are not truly sealed while cooling; an unpressurized vessel or container pulls in dirty air; blocks are susceptible as they cool toward 38 °C (100 °F).
Shipping containers with wooden floors, water troughs and leaky doors are 'an open buffet'. Hand-loading, dropped racks, barrels wheeled into clean areas add risk.

treat.v: Test: seal extra bags, cook and cool them with the batch, incubate unopened. Growth means dirty cool-down air.

prevent.v: Move blocks at 93 °C (200 °F) or more in racks, with welding gloves, straight into a positive-pressure HEPA room, below 38 °C in a few hours. Keep cool-down apart from incubation.
Cooling in a vessel back-pressurized with HEPA air is acceptable; the strictest practice never cools pasteurized blocks in the vessel.

spot.v: Recurring green, brown, black or orange moulds over months. Different moulds on settle plates in front of the hood. A rising rate of every contaminant despite a wall of flowhoods.

look.v: Technique alone can contaminate a whole lot: skin shedding, spawn bag held outside the flow, fingers in bags.

cause.v: Recirculating AC, heat pump or fan in the clean room; ceiling ducts blowing onto hoods; cheap 'HEPA' (99.7-99.9% instead of 99.999997%); damaged bottom edge of a mini-pleat filter; a switched-off filter soaking up humidity and spores; clogged pre-filters.
Traffic and removing bad bags in the same room as the knock table.

treat.v: Check pressure; plate-test or particle-count across the filter; inspect the bottom edge for breaks. Replace damaged filters. Observe first, then buy parts.

prevent.v: No recirculating units in the lab or cool-down room. Keep filters running, vacuum grain out of the base, add an angle-iron stop at the table edge, keep the room for one job.

risk.v: Chestnut and maitake lose first; lion's mane shows it early.

spot.v: Clumpy super sacks of supplement (probably wet once), flooded or mouldy sawdust piles, a wet pellet chunk stuck in a mixer that turned foul, sawdust arriving at about 70% moisture.

look.v: Properly hot-composted sawdust is effectively self-sanitized.

cause.v: Microbial load follows the moisture the material has seen. Soft-wood sawdust such as cedar suppresses mycelium. A nutrient-rich cake from a grimy mixer can survive steam.

treat.v: Do not use clumpy wet supplement. Measure incoming moisture. Clean mixers daily with an intensive weekly clean.

prevent.v: Store dry and indoors. Check the sawdust is the species ordered. Combo pellets worked better than raw sawdust after one flood.

risk.v: Lion's mane showed it first in the 70%-sawdust case.

spot.v: Patchy, odd colonization and failure to fruit.

look.v: Fermented grain gives splotchy growth too; check soak time first.

cause.v: Conventional millet and oats are often desiccated with glyphosate before harvest, and conventional rye may get fungicide. Supplier assurances may not be verifiable.

prevent.v: Use only organic grain, as Cap n Stem does.

spot.v: Patchy, splotchy, drying blocks; bags losing weight through the patch.

cause.v: Too much air exchange (CO2 about 500 ppm), for example from using the incubation HVAC to condition other rooms.

treat.v: Hold CO2 in the incubation band; give incubation its own HVAC.

prevent.v: Separate incubation HVAC; steady load in the room.
